To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
denervated Schwann cells of mechanoreceptors die by apoptosis, that this cell death can be prevented by glial growth factor (GGF), and that GGF is a neuregulin isoform.
Schwann cells associated mechanoreceptor terminals die after denervation in the early neonate, but that the Schwann cells can be rescued by glial growth factor, a soluble form of the neuregulins.
Schwann cells of mechanoreceptors die by apoptosis after denervation, and this can be prevented by glial growth factor, a soluble form of the neuregulins.
In summary, our research is concerned with
a novel mechanism of axon-Schwann cell interaction and its role in the re-establishement of peripheral mechanoreceptors.
the trophic interactions between axons and their target tissues, and the consequences of these interactions for axonal regeneration.
the role of neuregulins in the development and regeneration of mechanosensory end organs.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

Schwann cells are trophically-dependent on sensory axon-derived neuropeptides, and that the denervation-induced death and subsequent regeneration failure are correlated with deficiencies in Schwann cell trophic support.
the neuregulins are trophic to Schwann cells in sensory end organs, and that denervation-induced apoptosis is a major mechanism of the loss of these end organs after nerve injury.

Schwann cells associated to mechanoreceptors are trophically dependents of the axons and the axon-derived neuritegulins are the trophic factor that mediate the trophic interaction between Schwann cells and axon terminals.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
neuregulin/erbB signaling is a critical pathway in the formation of mechanoreceptors and that this pathway may be important for the re-establishment or regeneration of these mechanoreceptors.

Schwann cells of mechanoreceptors require neuregulin to prevent apoptosis and that the absence of this trophic factor may contribute to the failure of mechanoreceptors to re-establish after denervation.
Schwann cells associated mechanoreceptors in the developing peripheral nervous system are trophically maintained by sensory axon-derived glial growth factor.
The main takeaway from our work is that
Schwann cells are essential to the development of peripheral mechanoreceptors.

Schwann cells are trophically supported by sensory axons during early development and that the loss of this support leads to the death of Schwann cells and to the failure to re-establish mechanoreceptors after denervation.
Schwann cell death is a critical factor in the failure of regeneration of Golgi tendon organs.
